eventMetadata.context_description:
**Forecast models and official guidance from the Korea Meteorological Administration (KMA) currently favor a daytime high near 29–30 °C for Incheon International Airport on August 26, 2026, with Seoul proper running slightly warmer.** Persistent late-summer warmth combined with high humidity (often 70–90 %) and increasing cloud cover or scattered showers are the main drivers keeping peaks from climbing much higher, while light westerly winds limit further warming. Recent observations show daytime maxima in the 31–32 °C range on preceding days, but showers and overcast conditions on the 25th and 26th have introduced modest cooling that narrows the distribution toward the 29–31 °C band.  

Model consensus points to a peak in the early-to-mid afternoon, with resolution hinging on the exact timing and coverage of any showers and the degree of solar heating under partly cloudy skies. Traders have therefore concentrated probability on 30 °C (46 %) and 31 °C (32.5 %), with 29 °C still carrying meaningful weight (19.5 %) because any increase in cloudiness or precipitation could cap the high at that level. Higher outcomes above 32 °C remain low-probability because current steering patterns and moisture limit extreme heating. Updated KMA and numerical guidance issued closer to the event will be the key catalysts for any further shifts in these implied probabilities.

**Persistent subtropical high pressure is sustaining extreme heat across Chongqing ahead of August 26, with official forecasts from the Chongqing Meteorological Observatory projecting a city-wide high of 40°C and a center-city peak near 39°C under mostly clear to partly cloudy skies.**

Recent observations reinforce this setup: on August 25, multiple districts exceeded 37°C with a recorded peak of 39.9°C, continuing a pattern of consecutive hot days driven by the same high-pressure system. Topography (basin surrounded by mountains), urban heat island effects, and elevated humidity typical of the Yangtze River valley amplify surface temperatures, while light winds limit mixing. Scattered afternoon showers or thunderstorms, linked to peripheral influences from typhoons “Zitan” and “Jianlawei,” are expected mainly in southern districts and could locally cap the peak below 40°C at some monitoring sites.

Market-implied probabilities cluster on 38°C and 39°C because traders weigh the official 39–40°C guidance against historical variability in station-specific maxima and the moderating potential of convective rain. Model consensus and recent trend data favor the upper 30s as the most likely outcome for the official highest reading, with only modest probability assigned to 40°C or above given the timing of any showers. Updated forecast runs and any late-day precipitation reports will be the key near-term catalysts.

eventMetadata.context_description: **Consensus forecasts from the China Meteorological Administration and Hubei provincial meteorological services indicate a daytime high of 37–38°C in Wuhan on August 26 under mostly cloudy skies with scattered showers or thunderstorms.** Persistent subtropical high pressure over the Yangtze River basin, combined with strong late-August solar heating and relatively light winds, sustains the heat following one of the five hottest “Fu” periods (July 15–August 23) since 1961. Recent observations on August 25 already reached 37–38°C locally, reinforcing the short-term model consensus. Cooling associated with typhoon peripheral flow is not expected until after August 29, leaving August 26 largely unaffected. These official projections and the absence of significant model divergence explain the dominant market-implied probabilities clustered at 37–38°C.

**Forecast consensus from the National Weather Service and other models centers on a high of 103–105°F for Austin on August 26, 2026, under mostly sunny skies, light south-southwest winds, and continued dry conditions.** This aligns directly with the market’s heaviest weighting on the 102–103°F (53.5%) and 104–105°F (39.0%) bins. 

Late-August Central Texas typically features strong solar heating, low cloud cover, and southerly flow that advects warm, moderately humid air (dew points in the mid-60s), supporting afternoon temperatures in the low-to-mid 100s. A heat advisory remains in effect through the afternoon, with heat indices potentially reaching 107–109°F. Recent days have seen similar highs of 101–107°F without significant cooling trends or moisture influx that would cap temperatures lower. 

Slight model spread and local variations (urban heat island effects or exact timing of any thin clouds) keep the two central bins dominant, while the low probabilities assigned to extremes reflect the narrow uncertainty band around the official guidance. No major forecast shifts are anticipated before resolution.

**Strong high-pressure ridge and clear skies position Houston for another hot day on August 26, with official forecasts centering on highs near 100°F.** 

National Weather Service point forecasts and area matrices from the Houston/Galveston office indicate a maximum of 100°F (or 97–101°F depending on exact station), consistent with ongoing Heat Advisory conditions and heat indices of 106–109°F. Light southwest winds, minimal cloud cover, and low (0–10%) precipitation chances support efficient daytime heating under the ridge, pushing temperatures into the upper 90s to low 100s. 

Private forecasts align closely (WeatherBug at 99°F; others 99–102°F), reflecting model consensus on the ridge’s persistence before a weak disturbance increases rain chances and slightly lowers highs on Thursday. Historical August averages hover near 92–95°F, but 2026’s multi-week heat wave—with repeated 100°F readings—explains why traders assign the bulk of probability (over 95% combined) to the 98–101°F bins. Morning forecast updates or minor steering shifts could nudge the final observed high at the primary reporting station, but current data keep outcomes tightly clustered around the market leaders.

eventMetadata.context_description: **Southwest Monsoon conditions dominate Singapore's weather outlook for late August 2026, with official Meteorological Service Singapore guidance projecting daily maximum temperatures of 33–34°C on most days and occasional peaks to 35°C.** This climatological backdrop, combined with below-average rainfall and localized afternoon thundery showers, positions 32°C as the leading market outcome at 53.5% implied probability, followed by 31°C at 24.5%. Recent observations show highs frequently exceeding 33°C, yet short-range model runs for August 27 introduce modest uncertainty around convective cooling and wind patterns that could cap readings near 31–32°C. Traders weigh these factors against historical August maxima near 31.4°C and the narrow window before resolution, with fresh forecast updates from NEA and MSS likely to refine probabilities as the date approaches.

With resolution two days away, the close probabilities on 23–25°C reflect traders' assessment of this model consensus and the limited upside risk from stronger insolation. **Official forecasts from the Chongqing Municipal Meteorological Observatory position the highest temperature on August 27 near 38–39°C.** Persistent control by the subtropical high-pressure system continues to drive hot, mostly sunny conditions across much of the region, with recent daily peaks of 38–39.9°C on August 24–25 and a projected 40°C on the 26th. Scattered showers or thunderstorms, linked to peripheral flow from typhoon remnants, are expected mainly in southern and parts of central areas on the 27th, which could limit afternoon heating and cap the daily maximum around 38–39°C citywide (with center-city values near 38°C).

Global models show modest spread, with some ensembles indicating slightly lower peaks near 36–37°C under increased cloud cover or rain, while others align closer to the official outlook. Historical August patterns in Chongqing, where extremes often exceed 38°C during heatwaves, support the current clustering of market-implied probabilities around these values. Updated model runs and the next official briefing will likely refine the exact peak as the date approaches.

eventMetadata.context_description: **Persistent North Pacific high pressure, reinforced by a Tibetan heat dome, continues to drive elevated temperatures across southern South Korea, keeping Busan’s Aug. 27 maximum in the low-to-mid 30s Celsius range.** Recent KMA guidance and ensemble models show daytime peaks near 32–34 °C under partly cloudy skies, with a 40–60 % chance of afternoon thunderstorms that could briefly suppress readings by 1–2 °C or allow brief spikes if clearing occurs earlier. This narrow spread between 33 °C and 34 °C reflects uncertainty in convective timing and moisture advection from distant typhoons, which are steering humid air northward without direct landfall. Historical late-August climatology supports highs around 30–32 °C, so the current setup favors the market’s leading outcomes while leaving room for downward revision if showers arrive earlier or intensify.

eventMetadata.context_description:
**Recent forecasts from multiple models converge on a daytime high of 26–28°C for Amsterdam on August 27, 2026, with the market’s heaviest implied probabilities (27°C at 37%, 28°C at 23%, 26°C at 19.5%) reflecting this consensus.**

Easterly flow is maintaining relatively dry air in the short term, but increasing cloud cover and a shift toward southerly winds are expected to limit peak solar heating. Afternoon humidity is forecast to rise, supporting scattered showers or thunderstorms by evening that would further cap temperatures. This pattern aligns with a broader late-August cooling trend after warmer conditions earlier in the month.

Official guidance from sources such as GFS-based outputs and European models shows the highest readings most likely occurring in the early-to-mid afternoon before cloud build-up intensifies. Historical climatology places the late-August average high near 21–22°C, so the current setup represents modestly above-normal warmth tempered by increasing instability. Any revisions in the next 24–48 hours from updated model runs or observed trends in cloud cover and boundary-layer moisture will be the key variables that could shift the narrow 26–28°C window.

This market will resolve to the temperature range that contains the highest temperature recorded by NOAA at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport Station in degrees Celsius on 27 Aug '26.

The resolution source for this market will be information from NOAA, specifically the highest reading under the "Temp" column for all times on this day, available here: https://www.weather.gov/wrh/timeseries?site=rpll

If NOAA data is unavailable or missing for the observation period, Weather Underground will be used as the secondary resolution source.

To toggle between Fahrenheit and Celsius, click the "Switch to Metric Units" button until the relevant table displays °C.

This market can not resolve until the first data point for the following date has been published on the resolution source.

The resolution source for this market measures temperatures to whole degrees Celsius (eg, 9°C). Thus, this is the level of precision that will be used when resolving the market.

Revisions to temperatures recorded within this market's timeframe will be considered until the first datapoint for the following date has been published, after which any alterations will not be considered.

eventMetadata.context_description: **Persistent southwest monsoon flow and widespread cloud cover with scattered to frequent thunderstorms are the dominant factors capping daytime heating in Manila on August 27.** Official PAGASA guidance and multiple model runs project maximum temperatures of 29–31°C under mostly cloudy skies and moderate-to-strong southwesterly winds, with rainfall amounts sufficient to limit insolation and evaporative cooling. This aligns with the market’s leading outcomes at 31°C (41%), 30°C (25%), and 32°C (16.5%), reflecting trader consensus that monsoon-enhanced convection will prevent the higher 33–34°C readings occasionally seen in drier August periods. Short-term model updates through the next 48 hours, including any revisions to rainfall timing or intensity from PAGASA or global ensembles, remain the key variables that could shift the distribution slightly lower if heavier or more persistent showers materialize.
